paras: The 1915 Clay County manhunt was a search by a posse of up to 500 armed men, with bloodhounds, for an unnamed Black man accused of attacking Mrs. Henry Stafford in her farm home near Liberty, Clay County, Missouri, on August 5, 1915. Papers reported talk of lynching and predicted the man would be killed if caught, but the hounds lost the trail, rain ended the search on August 7, and no capture was reported. The hunt went out over the wires and was folded into roundups of a day of hangings and lynchings in the South, which the Chicago Defender reprinted under the headline "Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours."

According to a dispatch from Liberty, Mrs. Stafford, the wife of a farmer living four miles north of the town, was alone in the house with her baby when a man described as "a negro" entered, overpowered and gagged her, and bound her to a bed, where she was later found unconscious. Her husband was away with a threshing crew and her mother-in-law had gone to the mail box. Wire reports said she was in a "dangerous condition," while the Liberty dispatch said physicians expected her to recover. Most reports named her husband Henry Stafford, though a United Press dispatch called him Ned.

News of the attack spread through the neighborhood, threshing crews and farmers left their work, and within a short time at least 100 men and boys were out with weapons "bent on avenging the crime." A Kansas City dispatch said a posse had surrounded the southwestern corner of Clay County within two hours of Mrs. Stafford's discovery. About 300 men beat the brush southwest of Liberty through the night without sleep, and when relief parties arrived from Liberty and nearby towns on August 6 the posse grew to about 500.

The searchers enclosed a section seven miles square running toward the bend of the Missouri River at Kansas City, posted sentinels along the river and searched passing trains. Sheriff Seth White said he expected the man to be captured before noon on August 6. The United Press reported that the husband, carrying a shotgun, was "commanding the man hunt" behind the hounds, and the Topeka State Journal described the posse as excited, with talk of lynching heard often.

Late on August 6 the exhausted bloodhounds lost the trail, though officers kept their lines and a patrol on the river bank through the night. Rain on August 7 ended the search after about thirty-six hours. Police in Kansas City, Kansas, meanwhile held a man described as "crazy" or "insane" who matched the description in some details, and Sheriff White was asked to identify him, but the Topeka State Journal reported that he was not believed to be connected with the case.

A Kansas City dispatch of August 9 said news that Mrs. Stafford had suffered a "nervous breakdown" led residents of southern Clay County to renew the hunt with a fresh pack of bloodhounds. The same dispatch reported that almost $100,000 in rewards had been raised for the man's capture "dead or alive." No report of a capture, arrest or lynching appears in the coverage after that dispatch.

White papers carried the story as a wire item from Kansas City under headlines such as "Hunt for Negro," "Armed Men Pursue Negro" and "Mob Hunts for and Surrounds Black Man." The Topeka State Journal called the accused man a "fiend," and headlines in the Washington Evening Star and the Richmond Times-Dispatch called Mrs. Stafford a "white woman," presenting the attack as fact. The item ran from Washington to Florida and Oklahoma, and in German in the Detroiter Abend-Post under the heading "Lynchgericht droht." One-line digest versions of the United Press report were still appearing in Kentucky and Mississippi weeklies a week later.

On August 7 a Memphis roundup set the Liberty hunt beside seven legal hangings and two lynchings in the South, saying a "lynching party" was pursuing a tenth man. The New-York Tribune's version said he "probably will be caught and killed before morning," and the Milwaukee Leader wrote that a lynching was "almost certain."

The Black press reached the case only through that roundup. The Chicago Defender ran it on August 14 as a special from Memphis, with a subhead saying five of the deaths were "Cold Blooded Murders," and it replaced the wire's "negroes" with "Afro-Americans" and "member of the race." The Defender also called the man hunted near Liberty "supposed," a qualification absent from the white versions, and the Denver Star reprinted its text with credit on August 21.

The Liberty dispatch placed the attack on the morning of August 5, while the Kansas City wire said Thursday afternoon. Posse estimates ran from at least 100 in the first hours to about 300 overnight and 500 at the height of the search, figures that describe different stages of the hunt. The Topeka State Journal's headline said the man held in Kansas City, Kansas, "May Be Assailant," although its own text doubted any connection.

reader.title: 1915 Clay County manhunt
bases: A posse of up to 500 armed men hunted an accused Black man amid reported threats and talk of lynching, but no capture or killing was reported, making it a threatened lynching (A1, A2, A24).
A Liberty dispatch (A27), the Kansas City wire (A3, A4, A24) and the United Press (A2) agree on the alleged attack near Liberty and the armed posse with bloodhounds.

accounts.label: Liberty dispatch
accounts.gist: A man entered the house in the morning while Mrs. Stafford was alone with her baby, gagged and bound her; at least 100 armed men set out 'bent on avenging the crime.'

accounts.label: Kansas City wire
accounts.gist: Five hundred armed men surrounded the southwest corner of Clay County; the hounds lost the trail and rain ended the search on August 7; the hunt resumed about August 9 with large rewards.

accounts.label: United Press
accounts.gist: The husband, with a shotgun, commanded the hunt, and the man's life would 'be worth little' if the crowd overtook him.

accounts.label: Memphis roundup
accounts.gist: A 'lynching party' near Liberty was pursuing a tenth Black man after a day of seven legal hangings and two lynchings, and a lynching was 'almost certain.'

accounts.label: Black press rewrite
accounts.gist: The Defender recast the Memphis roundup as nine 'human beings hanged', calling five 'cold blooded murders', and repeated the Liberty sentence.

framing.detail: Kansas City wire ran under 'Hunt for Negro', 'Armed Men Pursue Negro' and 'Mob Hunts for and Surrounds Black Man', calling the accused a 'fiend' and the attack fact.
Memphis roundups listed the hunt with hangings and lynchings and forecast a lynching without comment.
The Defender's subhead called five of the deaths in the roundup 'Cold Blooded Murders' and it called the hunted man a 'supposed' member of the race.
The Denver Star reprinted the Defender version with credit.

conflicts.note: The Liberty dispatch is the local source; the afternoon time comes from the Kansas City wire.
Only the United Press used Ned; the Liberty dispatch and Kansas City wire say Henry.
Figures reflect different stages of the search rather than a contradiction; a raw OCR of A1 reads 800, but the re-read gives 300 and the posse 'swelled' to 500.
The Topeka State Journal's headline and its text differ.
